title: Early radio and records: Ross Gorman, Charley Johnson, Whiteman, Ellington
summary: As a boy he heard nightclub broadcasts, Charley Johnson's band, Paul Whiteman in theaters, and discovered Ellington on records, including the rumour that Tommy Dorsey was in Duke's band.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Can you remember any particular music you heard on the family phonograph that impressed you at an early age?

Well, at that particular age, if we're going to go back as far as that, seven or eight years old, that would be pretty hard to say. I used to hear broadcasts from the nightclubs, and of course they were -- the quality was ridiculous. But I remember hearing a saxophone player at the time, Ross Gorman, and he had an orchestra and he played at a club, I believe it was called the Monte Carlo Club. That was

back in the '20s, then I used to hear Charley Johnson's Orchestra, from Small's Paradise. Which also I was very impressed with. But they used to come on rather late, and I had to kind of sneak, you know, listening to them, because I was supposed to be in bed and asleep.
That was when you were probably how old, that you were listening to the nightclub shows?

Well, I would say this was maybe a little further on, around, oh, 10 or 12. But I remember being very impressed with the Charley Johnson Orchestra. And I remember my mother, she said, "I don't understand what you see in all that."
What particular part of the music impressed you? What did you like?

Well, I thought it was exciting, I mean, and interesting, and inventive. I mean it was different, let's put it that way. Of course then it was closely after that that I, through phonograph records, I became aware of the Ellington Orchestra. And that was really an extension of my interest in the Charley Johnson Orchestra, because the soloists in the Ellington Band, I mean, were so distinct, and they had such a distinct quality, that to me it was most interesting.
Did Charley Johnson's band -- I'm not -- I don't know about it, so, did it have interesting soloists also?

Well, they -- let's put it this way, it was a swinging band for that era. They had a drummer, I can't remember his last name, his name was George something, he was just excellent. And let's see, I don't know if they were in the band at that time, but at one time the trumpet players were Bill Coleman and Frank Newton. And it was, oh, I guess they had -- well, it was just like two trumpets and a trombone and three saxophones and four rhythm. It wasn't, you know, one of those huge bands. But none of the bands were at that time, except possibly Paul Whiteman.

Well, yeah, I used to go see him when he would play a theater or something like that, because I was too young to go into clubs. And I was impressed with Paul Whiteman. He was something to watch himself. I mean he was definitely the leader of the band, there was no question about that, and of course the band was so huge that it was -- you know, for that time, that alone was something that you just had to go see and hear.
So when did you -- you first heard Ellington, it would have been when he started the broadcast from --
No, I became aware of Ellington through records. I got ahold of some records. I can't remember who or where or when, but it was very early. And it sounded

different than anything that I'd ever heard, and I liked it. And I more or less kept buying them, you know, right on through the process where he went from the smaller band into the five brass and the four saxophone. I remember one time everybody on the street -- this was probably a little later -- they said, "Tommy Dorsey's playing with Duke Ellington." And I said, "You're kidding, he can't be." And what had happened, of course, Juan Tizol was the one, and Juan was very light in color and he wore the glasses, and the false rumor got out, you know, that Tommy Dorsey was playing trombone with Duke Ellington.
But his trombone didn't slide anymore, right?
